items: Conduct Physical Health Checks: Assess your cat's mobility and jumping ability for pain indicators such as hesitation before leaping, awkward landings, or using furniture to boost herself up instead of leaping directly.

Conduct Physical Health Checks: Evaluate your cat's grooming habits by comparing current behavior to normal, noting decreases, increases, or overgrooming that causes fur loss or skin irritation in specific areas.

Conduct Physical Health Checks: Monitor your cat's litterbox habits for warning signs including straining, crying, unusual time spent in the box, deposits outside the box, or changes in stool consistency and frequency.

Conduct Physical Health Checks: Observe your cat's resting posture for signs of discomfort such as frequently shifting positions, lying flat and extended instead of curled up, or avoiding specific body positions.

Document Behavioral Patterns: Establish a baseline of what normal behavior looks like for your specific cat before assessing changes, because two cats in the same household can have completely different normal baselines.

Document Behavioral Patterns: Build an escalation timeline that documents when the biting started, how it has progressed, and what circumstances preceded each escalation, because patterns reveal triggers you cannot see in your head.

Document Behavioral Patterns: Learn to recognize your cat's pre-attack body language by watching for subtle warning signals like ear position, tail movement, and whisker changes before aggression escalates to biting.

Document Behavioral Patterns: Map your cat's triggers across four environmental domains including resources, social dynamics, environmental stressors, and daily routine changes to identify what provokes the aggressive episodes.

Take Action With Your Vet: Schedule a veterinary appointment as the first priority after completing your physical assessment, because pain is the most common trigger for sudden aggression and must be ruled out first.

Take Action With Your Vet: Bring a prepared agenda to your veterinary visit that includes your completed 12-point pain assessment checklist, your escalation timeline, and specific observations about what you have witnessed.

Take Action With Your Vet: Ask your veterinarian to conduct a thorough pain evaluation during the exam, because cats hide pain brilliantly and what looks like a bad attitude is often a cat protecting herself from invisible discomfort.

Take Action With Your Vet: Create a targeted intervention plan that addresses the specific type of aggression your cat is displaying, because each of the six core aggression categories requires a different intervention approach.
